news.content_title: Overlapping Post-COVID Conditions: A Case of Myalgic Encephalomyelitis and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome Triggered by Sequential Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) Infections
news.content: Abstract The rise in post-infectious syndromes following COVID-19, such as Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), has become increasingly common in clinical practice, representing an emerging clinical challenge. This case highlights a possible clinical scenario involving the interaction between sequential viral infections - such as the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) - in triggering overlapping chronic conditions. This report presents the case of a patient who developed ME/CFS and POTS following SARS-CoV-2 infection, with a prior history of EBV mononucleosis, and discusses the diagnostic, therapeutic, and pathophysiological implications. A 48-year-old woman with a history of mononucleosis in childhood developed persistent and disabling symptoms after COVID-19 in January 2022. She presented with extreme fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, paresthesia, cognitive dysfunction, and multisystem symptoms. After extensive investigation, she was diagnosed with ME/CFS (early 2023) and POTS (later that year). Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) was considered as a hypothesis during follow-up, but objective testing was not confirmatory. Management included pharmacological therapy (including low-dose naltrexone, duloxetine, and palmitoylethanolamide (PEA)), activity adjustments (pacing), and a multidisciplinary approach, with partial and fluctuating responses. This case illustrates how viral infections such as EBV and SARS-CoV-2 may act as sequential triggers in an individual clinical trajectory compatible with the development of ME/CFS and POTS. The symptomatic overlap, the lack of readily available objective biomarkers in this patient, and the need for a predominantly clinical and functional diagnostic approach in her evaluation highlight the complexity of these conditions. This experience also underscores the importance of continued efforts in research, clinical training, and integrated care models to improve the management of patients presenting with post-COVID conditions (PCC). Introduction Myalgic Encephalomyelitis, also referred to as Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS), is a debilitating condition characterized by persistent and disabling fatigue without apparent cause, which does not improve with rest and worsens after physical or cognitive exertion. Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is a core symptom, often accompanied by cognitive impairment, musculoskeletal pain, and sleep disturbances, resulting in a significant impact on quality of life. The disease is more prevalent in women of reproductive age, with its main risk factors including previous viral infections (such as Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), positive family history, autoimmune diseases, intense physical or psychological stress, and associated chronic conditions such as fibromyalgia, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) [1,2]. On the other hand, POTS is a form of dysautonomia that frequently coexists with ME/CFS. It is characterized by orthostatic intolerance associated with an excessive increase in heart rate upon assuming an upright position, resulting in symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, and cognitive deficits. The overlap between ME/CFS and POTS is common and is associated with greater symptom intensity and worse clinical prognosis. Among the risk factors for POTS are a family history of dysautonomia, genetic predisposition, hormonal changes, and previous infections, such as mononucleosis (EBV), influenza, Lyme disease, and, more recently, COVID-19 [3-5]. These conditions share risk factors such as previous viral infections, genetic predisposition, and autoimmune diseases, suggesting an interaction between genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers [3-6]. Post-COVID conditions (PCC) are complex and multifaceted issues that arise after the acute phase of a SARS-CoV-2 infection. They are characterized by a diverse spectrum of new, recurrent, or persistent symptoms affecting multiple organ systems -such as neurological, cardiovascular, respiratory, and muscular - and which cannot be attributed to other diagnoses [7,8]. In addition to physical symptoms, studies report that many patients face intense post-pandemic emotional stress, exacerbated by uncertainty, isolation, and the burden of chronic illness [9,10]. There is also evidence that persistent inflammation may last for years after the initial infection, possibly contributing to prolonged symptomatology [11,12]. These symptoms typically manifest or persist for at least three months after the initial infection [7,8,13]. Beyond the physical impact, the condition carries profound mental, psychological, social, and economic consequences, including reduced work capacity, isolation, and diminished quality of life. Although its detailed pathophysiology remains under investigation, PCC represent a significant public health challenge, requiring a multidisciplinary approach to diagnosis, management, and support. Objective To report the case of a patient diagnosed with Myalgic Encephalomyelitis and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome who, following SARS-CoV-2 infection, developed persistent neurological, pulmonary, cardiac, cutaneous, and autonomic manifestations, resulting in significant functional impairment and reduced quality of life. Case Presentation The female patient had a history of six pregnancies, two deliveries, and four miscarriages. She was 48 years old, mixed-race, profession educator, and had a prior history of mononucleosis at age 11, hepatitis A at age 15, and an asthma diagnosis at age 20. The patient reported allergies to pineapple, kiwi, grapes, rosemary, oregano, eggplant, latex, shrimp, and other seafood. She experienced an episode of thrombophlebitis in her left upper limb at age 41. She denied any comorbidities prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection, as well as alcohol use and smoking. She engaged in regular physical exercise. The patient's clinical and temporal trajectory, from the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection through the evolution of PCC, diagnostic milestones, and therapeutic interventions, is detailed in Figure 1, which provides a graphical timeline of the case progression. The patient received the primary COVID-19 vaccination series with two doses of the Coronavac vaccine (SinoVac Biotech/Instituto Butantan) in early 2021. Subsequently, the first booster dose with the Comirnaty vaccine (Pfizer/BioNTech) was administered towards the end of the year followed by the second booster dose with the same vaccine in the middle of the next year. Thus, the patient completed the vaccination protocol, consisting of the primary series followed by two boosters. During the first consultation with our team on after two years at the Carlos Prates Health Center, the patient reported that her SARS-CoV-2 infection symptoms began more than two and half years earlier. They were initially mild and characterized by nasal congestion, malaise, and dry cough. COVID-19 was confirmed by RT-qPCR. Starting on the fourth day of symptoms, she experienced marked fatigue. During the acute phase, she used paracetamol and dipyrone sporadically. Due to the persistence of symptoms beyond 20 days, additional tests were requested, including a chest X-ray, which showed no changes compared to the initial presentation. At that time, corticosteroids and salbutamol were prescribed. New symptoms progressively emerged over the following weeks and months, including paresthesia in the lower and upper limbs, difficulty walking, sweating, cold extremities, bruising, urticaria, extreme physical and mental fatigue, insomnia, orthostatic intolerance, headache, digestive problems, shortness of breath while speaking and eating, intolerance to sound and light, low back pain, blurred vision, bladder pain, and dizziness. The patient sought specialized care in various fields, including Rheumatology, Neurology, Infectious Diseases, Pulmonology, Internal Medicine, Cardiology, Angiology, and Chinese Medicine. Most consultations were conducted in the private healthcare network, with respiratory rehabilitation carried out at the Sarah Kubitschek network in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. Several complementary tests were performed without detecting significant abnormalities, such as laboratory tests (renal and hepatic enzyme levels, electrolytes, serology for herpes virus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus, as well as urinalysis), function and imaging studies (spirometry, electroneuromyography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging), and other investigations (stool tests, pituitary hormone levels, thyroid hormones, and vitamin levels), all with results within normal parameters. Alternative diagnoses were systematically excluded through laboratory, imaging, and functional evaluations, all within normal limits. The PCC that had persisted for over three years since the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection included orthostatic intolerance, persistent fatigue, memory impairment, paresthesia in the lower and upper limbs, sweating and cold extremities, blurred vision, sensory hypersensitivity, insomnia, low back pain, bladder pain, gastroesophageal reflux, reduced hearing, and hair loss. The patient received diagnoses of PCC, i.e., ME/CFS in early 2023 and POTS at the end of the year. The diagnosis of ME/CFS was established according to the Institute of Medicine (IOM) 2015 diagnostic criteria (Systemic Exertion Intolerance Disease, SEID) [14]. The patient fulfilled all core criteria: (1) substantial reduction in pre-illness levels of occupational, educational, social, or personal activities, persisting for more than six months; (2) post-exertional malaise (PEM), documented by symptom worsening after light walking (10 minutes/day); (3) unrefreshing sleep; and (4) cognitive impairment and orthostatic intolerance, both present. POTS was confirmed by a head-up tilt-table test performed at an external cardiology service. Based on the medical report, the protocol involved head-up tilt at 70° for a passive phase of approximately 10 minutes. The diagnostic criterion applied was a sustained heart rate increment of ≥30 bpm within 10 minutes of upright posture, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension, accompanied by reproduction of the patient's orthostatic symptoms. Resting heart rate measurements obtained during subsequent follow-up visits were recorded as vital signs and were not used to establish the diagnosis of POTS. Regarding work, she was on medical leave for 45 days in mid-2022, returning towards the end of the same year after symptom stabilization. A year later, due to worsening condition, she was again placed on medical leave. Her therapeutic regimen included pyridostigmine bromide 60 mg (every 12 hours), duloxetine hydrochloride 60 mg/day, naltrexone 2 mg/day, bupropion 300 mg/day, palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) 600 mg/day, vitamin C 1 g/day, and Omega-3. During the second consultation with our team another year later, the patient reported that a rheumatologist in Belo Horizonte, consulted two months earlier, had reduced duloxetine hydrochloride to 30 mg and increased PEA to 900 mg/day, and that she experienced worsening of symptoms after starting light walks (10 minutes/day). In the third consultation two months later, the patient reported another visit to the rheumatologist (end of the year), who increased PEA to 1200 mg/day, and to a psychiatrist (end of the year), who maintained bupropion 300 mg/day, naltrexone 2 mg/day, and duloxetine hydrochloride 30 mg/day. She reported partial improvement in fatigue, orthostatic symptoms, and memory, but worsening of hair loss. She discontinued acupuncture, started hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg/day for gastric and post-exertional symptoms, and continued the walks. During the fourth consultation early next year, a worsening of her condition was observed following a trip, with increased physical and cognitive fatigue, reduced domestic and leisure activities, and more frequent flu-like symptoms. Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) was considered as a diagnostic hypothesis, but no objective testing was available to confirm it; therefore, it remains speculative and unconfirmed. The patient consulted a new rheumatologist in São Paulo, Brazil, who requested tests and proposed pulse therapy, as well as an infectious disease specialist next month, who maintained the physiotherapy sessions. In the last consultation with our team during monitoring in mid-2025, the patient reported starting pulse therapy with methylprednisolone 125 mg/day for three days, initiated on five months earlier, and treatment with vitamin B12 1 mg/day two months earlier. The patient was prospectively evaluated and followed in person by the authors at our facility, and the information in this report was obtained during these consultations, complemented by review of medical records. Detailed data obtained during the clinical consultations and follow-up visits are provided in Table 1. These consultations were conducted as part of a clinical study called VITA Monitoring, which is responsible for following 212 individuals with PCC under the coordination of the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation and in partnership with the Brazilian Ministry of Health and the Belo Horizonte Municipal Health Department. The consultations took place at the Carlos Prates Health Center in Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil. VITA Monitoring is an 18-month cohort with five in-person consultations and telephone follow-ups, including clinical and laboratory analyses. This work reports follow-up data at multiple time points: baseline (V1) and evaluations after one month (1M), three months (3M), six months (6M), and twelve months (12M), conducted from mid-2024 onwards for a year. Written informed consent for publication of this case report and any accompanying images was obtained from the patient. Discussion This case illustrates the complex interaction between viral infections, individual predisposition, and the emergence of chronic overlapping syndromes such as ME/CFS and POTS. The patient had a significant history of prior EBV infection in childhood, a well-established risk factor for the development of post-infectious diseases. Subsequently, the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection acted as a potent secondary triggering event, generating a cascade of persistent and debilitating symptoms. This scenario supports the double-hit vulnerability model, in which an initial viral infection predisposes the immune and neurological systems, while a second insult triggers the full clinical syndrome. The high prevalence of ME/CFS and POTS in post-COVID cohorts reinforces the role of SARS-CoV-2 as a predominant trigger in the current era, suggesting common pathophysiological mechanisms such as autonomic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and abnormal immune activation [15,16]. The patient's diagnostic journey, which involved multiple specialties and extensive evaluation through complementary tests with normal results, reflects one of the greatest challenges in managing ME/CFS and POTS: the difficulty of applying conventional tests. The absence of specific biochemical or imaging markers often leads to diagnostic delays, disbelief from some healthcare professionals, and additional suffering for the patient. This case highlights the crucial importance of established clinical criteria and functional tests, such as the Tilt Test for POTS and the assessment of PEM for ME/CFS. The diagnosis therefore remains grounded in careful history-taking and recognition of characteristic symptomatic patterns. This reinforces the urgent need for greater clinical training so that healthcare professionals understand that PCCs are real and diverse entities, and must be alert and sensitive to the profile of a significant portion of patients who, like the one described, present with severe illness in the absence of classic laboratory abnormalities. MCAS was considered as a possible unifying mechanism for the patient's multisystem symptoms, including urticaria, gastrointestinal complaints, intolerances, fatigue, and brain fog. However, no objective testing (serum tryptase, urinary histamine metabolites) was performed or confirmatory in this case. Therefore, MCAS remains an unconfirmed hypothesis and should be interpreted with caution. Growing evidence suggests an association between MCAS and PCC, ME/CFS, and POTS [17,18], but further objective testing is needed before drawing definitive conclusions. From a therapeutic standpoint, the management of ME/CFS and PCC with POTS is characterized by an empirical and multidisciplinary approach, largely guided by real-world evidence reported by patients. For POTS, this systematic review highlights interventions such as compression stockings and salt supplementation as first-line non-pharmacological approaches that improve symptoms and hemodynamics, while ivabradine and beta-adrenergic blockers (such as propranolol and bisoprolol) showed strong evidence among pharmacological options. In parallel, recent studies on ME/CFS highlight other interventions with consistently positive responses: pacing, considered the strategy with the highest perceived benefit, especially improves fatigue, PEM, and brain fog; low-dose naltrexone leading to significant results in the same symptoms, albeit with a limited effect on POTS; and intravenous or subcutaneous immunoglobulin (IgG) with broad benefits, including for fatigue, post-exertional malaise, POTS, and brain fog, particularly in patients with multisystem symptoms [16,19]. The prescribed medication regimen combined neuromodulators, an anti-inflammatory agent (PEA), and attempts at immune modulation (corticosteroid pulse therapy). This case illustrates how viral infections such as EBV and SARS-CoV-2 may act as sequential triggers in an individual clinical trajectory compatible with the development of ME/CFS and POTS. The symptomatic overlap, the lack of readily available objective biomarkers in this patient, and the need for a predominantly clinical and functional diagnostic approach in her evaluation highlight the complexity of these conditions. This experience also underscores the importance of continued efforts in research, clinical training, and integrated care models to improve the management of patients presenting with post-COVID conditions (PCC). Introduction Myalgic Encephalomyelitis, also referred to as Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS), is a debilitating condition characterized by persistent and disabling fatigue without apparent cause, which does not improve with rest and worsens after physical or cognitive exertion. Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is a core symptom, often accompanied by cognitive impairment, musculoskeletal pain, and sleep disturbances, resulting in a significant impact on quality of life. The disease is more prevalent in women of reproductive age, with its main risk factors including previous viral infections (such as Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), positive family history, autoimmune diseases, intense physical or psychological stress, and associated chronic conditions such as fibromyalgia, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) [1,2]. On the other hand, POTS is a form of dysautonomia that frequently coexists with ME/CFS. It is characterized by orthostatic intolerance associated with an excessive increase in heart rate upon assuming an upright position, resulting in symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, and cognitive deficits. The overlap between ME/CFS and POTS is common and is associated with greater symptom intensity and worse clinical prognosis. Among the risk factors for POTS are a family history of dysautonomia, genetic predisposition, hormonal changes, and previous infections, such as mononucleosis (EBV), influenza, Lyme disease, and, more recently, COVID-19 [3-5]. These conditions share risk factors such as previous viral infections, genetic predisposition, and autoimmune diseases, suggesting an interaction between genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers [3-6]. Post-COVID conditions (PCC) are complex and multifaceted issues that arise after the acute phase of a SARS-CoV-2 infection. They are characterized by a diverse spectrum of new, recurrent, or persistent symptoms affecting multiple organ systems -such as neurological, cardiovascular, respiratory, and muscular - and which cannot be attributed to other diagnoses [7,8]. In addition to physical symptoms, studies report that many patients face intense post-pandemic emotional stress, exacerbated by uncertainty, isolation, and the burden of chronic illness [9,10]. There is also evidence that persistent inflammation may last for years after the initial infection, possibly contributing to prolonged symptomatology [11,12]. These symptoms typically manifest or persist for at least three months after the initial infection [7,8,13]. Beyond the physical impact, the condition carries profound mental, psychological, social, and economic consequences, including reduced work capacity, isolation, and diminished quality of life. Although its detailed pathophysiology remains under investigation, PCC represent a significant public health challenge, requiring a multidisciplinary approach to diagnosis, management, and support. Objective To report the case of a patient diagnosed with Myalgic Encephalomyelitis and Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome who, following SARS-CoV-2 infection, developed persistent neurological, pulmonary, cardiac, cutaneous, and autonomic manifestations, resulting in significant functional impairment and reduced quality of life. Case Presentation The female patient had a history of six pregnancies, two deliveries, and four miscarriages. She was 48 years old, mixed-race, profession educator, and had a prior history of mononucleosis at age 11, hepatitis A at age 15, and an asthma diagnosis at age 20. The patient reported allergies to pineapple, kiwi, grapes, rosemary, oregano, eggplant, latex, shrimp, and other seafood. She experienced an episode of thrombophlebitis in her left upper limb at age 41. She denied any comorbidities prior to SARS-CoV-2 infection, as well as alcohol use and smoking. She engaged in regular physical exercise. The patient's clinical and temporal trajectory, from the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection through the evolution of PCC, diagnostic milestones, and therapeutic interventions, is detailed in Figure 1, which provides a graphical timeline of the case progression. The patient received the primary COVID-19 vaccination series with two doses of the Coronavac vaccine (SinoVac Biotech/Instituto Butantan) in early 2021. Subsequently, the first booster dose with the Comirnaty vaccine (Pfizer/BioNTech) was administered towards the end of the year followed by the second booster dose with the same vaccine in the middle of the next year. Thus, the patient completed the vaccination protocol, consisting of the primary series followed by two boosters. During the first consultation with our team on after two years at the Carlos Prates Health Center, the patient reported that her SARS-CoV-2 infection symptoms began more than two and half years earlier. They were initially mild and characterized by nasal congestion, malaise, and dry cough. COVID-19 was confirmed by RT-qPCR. Starting on the fourth day of symptoms, she experienced marked fatigue. During the acute phase, she used paracetamol and dipyrone sporadically. Due to the persistence of symptoms beyond 20 days, additional tests were requested, including a chest X-ray, which showed no changes compared to the initial presentation. At that time, corticosteroids and salbutamol were prescribed. New symptoms progressively emerged over the following weeks and months, including paresthesia in the lower and upper limbs, difficulty walking, sweating, cold extremities, bruising, urticaria, extreme physical and mental fatigue, insomnia, orthostatic intolerance, headache, digestive problems, shortness of breath while speaking and eating, intolerance to sound and light, low back pain, blurred vision, bladder pain, and dizziness. The patient sought specialized care in various fields, including Rheumatology, Neurology, Infectious Diseases, Pulmonology, Internal Medicine, Cardiology, Angiology, and Chinese Medicine. Most consultations were conducted in the private healthcare network, with respiratory rehabilitation carried out at the Sarah Kubitschek network in Belo Horizonte, Brazil. Several complementary tests were performed without detecting significant abnormalities, such as laboratory tests (renal and hepatic enzyme levels, electrolytes, serology for herpes virus, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus, as well as urinalysis), function and imaging studies (spirometry, electroneuromyography, and brain magnetic resonance imaging), and other investigations (stool tests, pituitary hormone levels, thyroid hormones, and vitamin levels), all with results within normal parameters. Alternative diagnoses were systematically excluded through laboratory, imaging, and functional evaluations, all within normal limits. The PCC that had persisted for over three years since the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection included orthostatic intolerance, persistent fatigue, memory impairment, paresthesia in the lower and upper limbs, sweating and cold extremities, blurred vision, sensory hypersensitivity, insomnia, low back pain, bladder pain, gastroesophageal reflux, reduced hearing, and hair loss. The patient received diagnoses of PCC, i.e., ME/CFS in early 2023 and POTS at the end of the year. The diagnosis of ME/CFS was established according to the Institute of Medicine (IOM) 2015 diagnostic criteria (Systemic Exertion Intolerance Disease, SEID) [14]. The patient fulfilled all core criteria: (1) substantial reduction in pre-illness levels of occupational, educational, social, or personal activities, persisting for more than six months; (2) post-exertional malaise (PEM), documented by symptom worsening after light walking (10 minutes/day); (3) unrefreshing sleep; and (4) cognitive impairment and orthostatic intolerance, both present. POTS was confirmed by a head-up tilt-table test performed at an external cardiology service. Based on the medical report, the protocol involved head-up tilt at 70° for a passive phase of approximately 10 minutes. The diagnostic criterion applied was a sustained heart rate increment of ≥30 bpm within 10 minutes of upright posture, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension, accompanied by reproduction of the patient's orthostatic symptoms. Resting heart rate measurements obtained during subsequent follow-up visits were recorded as vital signs and were not used to establish the diagnosis of POTS. Regarding work, she was on medical leave for 45 days in mid-2022, returning towards the end of the same year after symptom stabilization. A year later, due to worsening condition, she was again placed on medical leave. Her therapeutic regimen included pyridostigmine bromide 60 mg (every 12 hours), duloxetine hydrochloride 60 mg/day, naltrexone 2 mg/day, bupropion 300 mg/day, palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) 600 mg/day, vitamin C 1 g/day, and Omega-3. During the second consultation with our team another year later, the patient reported that a rheumatologist in Belo Horizonte, consulted two months earlier, had reduced duloxetine hydrochloride to 30 mg and increased PEA to 900 mg/day, and that she experienced worsening of symptoms after starting light walks (10 minutes/day). In the third consultation two months later, the patient reported another visit to the rheumatologist (end of the year), who increased PEA to 1200 mg/day, and to a psychiatrist (end of the year), who maintained bupropion 300 mg/day, naltrexone 2 mg/day, and duloxetine hydrochloride 30 mg/day. She reported partial improvement in fatigue, orthostatic symptoms, and memory, but worsening of hair loss. She discontinued acupuncture, started hydroxyzine hydrochloride 25 mg/day for gastric and post-exertional symptoms, and continued the walks. During the fourth consultation early next year, a worsening of her condition was observed following a trip, with increased physical and cognitive fatigue, reduced domestic and leisure activities, and more frequent flu-like symptoms. Mast Cell Activation Syndrome (MCAS) was considered as a diagnostic hypothesis, but no objective testing was available to confirm it; therefore, it remains speculative and unconfirmed. The patient consulted a new rheumatologist in São Paulo, Brazil, who requested tests and proposed pulse therapy, as well as an infectious disease specialist next month, who maintained the physiotherapy sessions. In the last consultation with our team during monitoring in mid-2025, the patient reported starting pulse therapy with methylprednisolone 125 mg/day for three days, initiated on five months earlier, and treatment with vitamin B12 1 mg/day two months earlier. The patient was prospectively evaluated and followed in person by the authors at our facility, and the information in this report was obtained during these consultations, complemented by review of medical records. Detailed data obtained during the clinical consultations and follow-up visits are provided in Table 1. These consultations were conducted as part of a clinical study called VITA Monitoring, which is responsible for following 212 individuals with PCC under the coordination of the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation and in partnership with the Brazilian Ministry of Health and the Belo Horizonte Municipal Health Department. The consultations took place at the Carlos Prates Health Center in Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil. VITA Monitoring is an 18-month cohort with five in-person consultations and telephone follow-ups, including clinical and laboratory analyses. This work reports follow-up data at multiple time points: baseline (V1) and evaluations after one month (1M), three months (3M), six months (6M), and twelve months (12M), conducted from mid-2024 onwards for a year. Written informed consent for publication of this case report and any accompanying images was obtained from the patient. Discussion This case illustrates the complex interaction between viral infections, individual predisposition, and the emergence of chronic overlapping syndromes such as ME/CFS and POTS. The patient had a significant history of prior EBV infection in childhood, a well-established risk factor for the development of post-infectious diseases. Subsequently, the acute SARS-CoV-2 infection acted as a potent secondary triggering event, generating a cascade of persistent and debilitating symptoms. This scenario supports the double-hit vulnerability model, in which an initial viral infection predisposes the immune and neurological systems, while a second insult triggers the full clinical syndrome. The high prevalence of ME/CFS and POTS in post-COVID cohorts reinforces the role of SARS-CoV-2 as a predominant trigger in the current era, suggesting common pathophysiological mechanisms such as autonomic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and abnormal immune activation [15,16]. The patient's diagnostic journey, which involved multiple specialties and extensive evaluation through complementary tests with normal results, reflects one of the greatest challenges in managing ME/CFS and POTS: the difficulty of applying conventional tests. The absence of specific biochemical or imaging markers often leads to diagnostic delays, disbelief from some healthcare professionals, and additional suffering for the patient. This case highlights the crucial importance of established clinical criteria and functional tests, such as the Tilt Test for POTS and the assessment of PEM for ME/CFS. The diagnosis therefore remains grounded in careful history-taking and recognition of characteristic symptomatic patterns. This reinforces the urgent need for greater clinical training so that healthcare professionals understand that PCCs are real and diverse entities, and must be alert and sensitive to the profile of a significant portion of patients who, like the one described, present with severe illness in the absence of classic laboratory abnormalities. MCAS was considered as a possible unifying mechanism for the patient's multisystem symptoms, including urticaria, gastrointestinal complaints, intolerances, fatigue, and brain fog. However, no objective testing (serum tryptase, urinary histamine metabolites) was performed or confirmatory in this case. Therefore, MCAS remains an unconfirmed hypothesis and should be interpreted with caution. Growing evidence suggests an association between MCAS and PCC, ME/CFS, and POTS [17,18], but further objective testing is needed before drawing definitive conclusions. From a therapeutic standpoint, the management of ME/CFS and PCC with POTS is characterized by an empirical and multidisciplinary approach, largely guided by real-world evidence reported by patients. For POTS, this systematic review highlights interventions such as compression stockings and salt supplementation as first-line non-pharmacological approaches that improve symptoms and hemodynamics, while ivabradine and beta-adrenergic blockers (such as propranolol and bisoprolol) showed strong evidence among pharmacological options. In parallel, recent studies on ME/CFS highlight other interventions with consistently positive responses: pacing, considered the strategy with the highest perceived benefit, especially improves fatigue, PEM, and brain fog; low-dose naltrexone leading to significant results in the same symptoms, albeit with a limited effect on POTS; and intravenous or subcutaneous immunoglobulin (IgG) with broad benefits, including for fatigue, post-exertional malaise, POTS, and brain fog, particularly in patients with multisystem symptoms [16,19]. The prescribed medication regimen combined neuromodulators, an anti-inflammatory agent (PEA), and attempts at immune modulation (corticosteroid pulse therapy). news.content_zh: 本报告描述了一名 48 岁女性病例,她于 2022 年 1 月感染 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 后出现肌痛性脑脊髓炎/慢性疲劳综合征 (ME/CFS) 和体位性心动过速综合征 (POTS)。她既往有 Epstein-Barr 病毒 (EBV) 单核细胞增多症病史。患者出现持续的致残症状,包括极度疲劳、直立不耐受、感觉异常、认知功能障碍和多系统表现。这些症状严重影响了她的生活质量和功能能力。她于 2023 年初被诊断出患有 ME/CFS,并于同年晚些时候被诊断出患有 POTS。该病例凸显了新冠肺炎后病症 (PCC) 的复杂性,其特点是影响多个器官系统的各种新的、复发的或持续的症状。该报告强调了对 诊断 和管理采取多学科方法的必要性,以及确定这些病症的客观生物标志物的挑战。该研究还强调了持续研究和临床培训的重要性,以更好地解决 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染的长期影响。

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：该患者在2022年1月感染严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2后出现症状，于2023年初出现ME/CFS症状，同年晚些时候出现POTS症...；地点与对象：该病例是在临床环境中报告的，患者是一名 48 岁女性，童年有单核细胞增多症病史。证据中没有指明具体地点。；事件：一例 严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2 感染后出现肌痛性脑脊髓炎/慢性疲劳综合征 (ME/CFS) 和体位性心动过速综合征 (POTS) 的患者，既往有 Epstein-Barr 病毒 (EBV) 单核细胞增多症病史。这是该文章作者报道的一个确诊的临床...；影响与风险：患者出现持续性和致残症状，包括极度疲劳、直立不耐受、感觉异常、认知功能障碍和多系统症状。这些情况严重影响了她的生活质量和功能能力。该报告没有提供具体病例或死亡人数，但强调了新冠疫情后状况的复杂性和严重性。；应对与不确定性：患者接受了多学科治疗方法，包括药物治疗和活动调整。诊断 通过临床评估得到证实，该病例作为诊断和管理新冠肺炎后病情挑战的一个例子。调查范围广泛，但没有客观测试证实所有假设，包括肥大细胞激活综合征(MCAS)。

The research examines the use of machine learning to analyze plasma proteomics and single-cell immune data related to COVID-19 severity. The work identified potential markers and explored an approach that could be extended to future research in environmental and viral immunology. This aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal #3: Good Health and Well-Being. Lynn alumni Tashoy Campbell '25 and Megan Ramsey '22, '26 contributed to the project. news.content: Skip to Main Content Johns Hopkins Medicine Menu Health School of Medicine Johns Hopkins Medicine Home About Patient Care Research MyChart Schedule an Appointment Find a Doctor Find a Clinical Trial Pay Your Bill Employment Close Search Search Johns Hopkins Medicine Search Close MyChart Login MyChart Health Health Menu Health Main Menu Health Home Conditions and Diseases Treatments, Tests and Therapies Wellness and Prevention Caregiving Home Health Home Wellness and Prevention 2026–27 Flu, COVID-19 and RSV Vaccine Recommendations Infectious Diseases Influenza COVID-19 Published September 25, 2026 As the weather cools and people spend more time indoors, common viruses — including those that cause the flu, COVID-19 and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) — have opportunities to spread and infect their hosts. To help people of all ages safeguard against seasonal illness, physicians and experts at Johns Hopkins Medicine share strategies to support optimal health. Key Points Flu season starts near the end of October, so it’s a good to get vaccinated soon (per guidelines below) for flu, COVID-19 and RSV. You can take steps to reduce the risk of infection. Treatments can relieve symptoms and shorten the duration of illness. Talk to your healthcare provider about specific questions or concerns. Flu (Influenza) Vaccine Recommendations The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that most people age 6 months and older receive an annual flu vaccine. Vaccination before the end of October is ideal, but vaccination later in the season can still offer protection. Here are a few things to remember about the flu vaccine: It’s never too late: The flu vaccine takes about two weeks to help train your body how to recognize and respond to influenza, so it’s never too late to get an updated vaccine — you can do it at any time during the flu season, which tends to peak between December and February and can extend through May. What’s new: All flu vaccines for the 2026–27 season were designed to protect against three different influenza viruses: two influenza A viruses and an influenza B/Victoria virus. A newly approved mRNA flu vaccine (mFLUSIVA) is available for adults age 50 and older. Flu Vaccine Recommendation by Age Most people age 6 months and older should get an annual, age-appropriate flu vaccine: Children ages 6 months to 8 years should get one or two doses. Two doses are necessary for children: Who have never received a flu vaccine. Whose vaccine history is unknown. Who received the vaccine before but not according to the recommended schedule (two doses given at least four weeks apart). Children age 9 years and older should get one dose. Flu Vaccine Options When it comes to the flu, different vaccine options — including flu shots and a nasal spray — are available. Similar to other viruses, flu vaccine types and dosing vary based on a person’s age, their underlying health conditions and risks for severe illness, as well as personal preferences. Common flu vaccine options include: Egg- or cell-based flu shots (appropriate for many age groups). A new mRNA vaccine for adults age 50 and older. For adults age 65 and older, CDC recommends higher-dose flu vaccines (including high-dose inactivated and recombinant vaccines) or adjuvanted inactivated flu vaccine. A nasal spray flu vaccine is an option for people ages 2 through 49 who are not pregnant and who do not have underlying health conditions. What treatments are available if I get the flu? Antiviral medications are available for children and adults. These medicines work best when taken within two days of getting first symptoms. Over-the-counter medications can be used to treat pain and reduce fevers, but children and teens should take acetaminophen (not aspirin). People with severe illness and/or complications from the flu may need additional care, including breathing assistance, extra hydration and other medications to support recovery. Can I get flu and COVID vaccines at the same time? Yes, most people can safely get the flu and COVID-19 vaccines during the same visit. If you are getting shots for both, they may be given in different arms. As with any vaccine, you may experience temporary side effects such as soreness at the injection site, fatigue, headache and muscle aches. However, the side effects after getting both vaccines together are generally similar to those seen when the vaccines are given separately. And if you are eligible for the RSV vaccine, you can get all three during the same visit. If you have questions about the best timing based on your age and health conditions, talk with your healthcare provider. COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) Vaccine Recommendations COVID-19 vaccines help protect against severe illness, hospitalization and death. Each year, the COVID-19 vaccine is updated to target the most relevant strains of the virus. Johns Hopkins Medicine recommends all individuals 6 months and older receive the 2026–27 COVID-19 vaccine. This recommendation is based on assessments within our organization and review of medical data. Check with your healthcare provider if you have questions specific to your health needs. Vaccination is especially important for: Adults 65 and older. People at high risk for severe COVID-19, such as those who are immunocompromised. Long-term-care residents. People who have never been vaccinated against COVID-19. People who are pregnant or planning pregnancy. Children ages 6–23 months. COVID-19 Vaccine Options There are several COVID-19 vaccine options. People can choose from mRNA vaccines (e.g., Moderna or Pfizer-BioNTech) or a protein-based vaccine (e.g., Novavax), depending on the person’s age and vaccine availability: Moderna’s mRNA (Spikevax) vaccine can be given to anyone 6 months and over. Pfizer’s mRNA vaccine (Comirnaty) can be given to anyone 5 years and over. Moderna’s lower-dose mRNA vaccine (mNexspike) can be given to anyone 12 years and over. Novavax’s protein-based vaccine (Nuvaxovid) can be given to anyone 12 years and over. What treatments are available if I get COVID-19? Antiviral medications can help reduce the risk of severe illness, hospitalization and death in people who are at higher risk for complications from COVID-19. These treatments work best when started within five to seven days after symptoms begin. If you test positive for COVID-19 and are at increased risk for severe illness, contact your healthcare provider as soon as possible to discuss whether antiviral medications are right for you. People with severe illness and/or complications from COVID-19 may need additional care, including breathing assistance, extra hydration and other medications to support recovery. RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) Vaccine Recommendations RSV vaccine recommendations vary by age: Women who are pregnant should get an RSV vaccine between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy to protect the baby after birth. If the mother did not get the RSV vaccine during pregnancy, if her vaccination status is unknown or if the baby was born within 14 days of the vaccination, the baby may need a long-acting RSV antibody (not a vaccine) before 8 months of age. Some children ages 8 to 19 months who are at an increased risk for severe RSV disease should receive the RSV antibody before their second RSV season (October through March). Adults age 75 and older should receive a single dose of an RSV vaccine. Adults ages 50–74 who are at increased risk for severe RSV disease should also receive a single dose. RSV vaccination is currently a one-time recommendation for eligible adults. People who have already received an RSV vaccine, even in a previous year, do not need another dose. Over-the-counter medications can be used to treat pain and reduce fevers, but children and teens should take acetaminophen (not aspirin). People with severe illness and/or complications from RSV may need additional care, including breathing assistance, extra hydration and other medications to support recovery. Tips to Reduce Risk of Flu, COVID-19 or RSV Use good hand-washing practices, such as washing hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Use hand sanitizer when soap and water aren’t an option. If possible, plan activities with large groups of people outdoors or in well-ventilated areas. Wear a well-fitted mask when in a crowded indoor setting or when around people who are sick. Sneeze or cough into your elbow when around other people. Stay away from people if you become sick, and avoid being around people who are sick, if possible. Stay hydrated, and prioritize getting adequate sleep to support immune function. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Sunday, September 27, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Biology SARS-CoV-2 Enzyme NSP14 Disrupts DHX15-RIG-I Partnership to Silence Antiviral Alarm by Bioengineer September 25, 2026 in Biology Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram When a virus slips into a human cell, the first hours of infection decide much of what follows. The cell’s pattern recognition receptors scan the cytoplasm for molecular signatures that betray an invader, chief among them double-stranded RNA, and one of the most important sentinels in this surveillance system is the retinoic acid-inducible gene I, known widely as RIG-I. Once RIG-I binds viral RNA, it initiates a signaling cascade that culminates in the production of type I and type III interferons, the cytokines that place neighboring cells on heightened alert and coordinate the antiviral response. SARS-CoV-2, the agent responsible for COVID-19, has proven remarkably adept at delaying or blunting this alarm, and a study published in Virology Journal now adds a detailed mechanism to the growing catalog of its evasion strategies. The work, led by researchers at Guizhou Medical University, focuses on nonstructural protein 14, or NSP14, and reveals how this multifunctional viral enzyme quietly severs a critical partnership that amplifies interferon signaling. NSP14 is one of sixteen nonstructural proteins encoded by the SARS-CoV-2 genome, and it wears two enzymatic hats that are both essential for viral replication. Its N-terminal domain functions as an exoribonuclease, proofreading freshly synthesized viral RNA and excising mismatched nucleotides, while its C-terminal domain acts as an N7-methyltransferase, adding a methyl group to the 5′ cap of viral messenger RNA so that the RNA masquerades as a cellular transcript. This cap modification allows viral RNA to evade detection by innate immune receptors and to be translated efficiently by the host machinery. Previous research had implicated NSP14 in antagonizing interferon responses, but the precise route it takes through the signaling network remained incompletely mapped, particularly with respect to the RIG-I pathway that dominates the sensing of RNA viruses. To dissect this question, the research team employed overexpression systems and reporter assays to test what happens to interferon production when NSP14 is present. The results were unambiguous. Elevated levels of NSP14 significantly suppressed both type I and type III interferon responses, along with the expression of downstream interferon-stimulated genes, the effector proteins that execute much of the antiviral program. The suppression extended to key signaling intermediates: activation of TBK1, the kinase that phosphorylates downstream transcription factors, and activation of IRF3, the transcription factor that drives interferon-beta transcription, were both dampened. In effect, NSP14 was acting upstream of the phosphorylation events that normally convert RNA sensing into gene expression, placing its point of interference early in the RIG-I signaling axis. Discover more Covid-19 Infectious Diseases Medical Literature & Resources Drugs & Medications Respiratory Conditions A central question in such experiments is which part of a viral protein carries out a given function, and the team addressed this by testing whether NSP14’s immunosuppressive effect depended on its catalytic activities or on its interactions with other viral components. NSP14 is known to form a complex with NSP10, a cofactor that stimulates its exoribonuclease activity, and the researchers examined whether this partnership was required. It was not. The inhibitory effect on RIG-I-mediated antiviral signaling persisted independently of complex formation with NSP10. What did matter was the C-terminal N7-methyltransferase activity. When that function was disabled, the ability of NSP14 to suppress interferon production was lost, indicating that the methyltransferase domain is the business end of the immune evasion strategy, even though the mechanism does not appear to operate through cap modification of viral RNA itself. With the functional requirement mapped to the methyltransferase domain, the investigators turned to the question of which host protein NSP14 might be targeting. Using immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry, they searched for cellular interaction partners of NSP14 and identified DHX15, a DEAH-box helicase that had previously been characterized as a co-receptor of RIG-I. DHX15 belongs to the large family of DExD/C-box helicases, enzymes that remodel RNA structures and, in several cases, contribute to innate immune signaling. The finding that a viral enzyme with methyltransferase activity physically contacts DHX15 suggested a plausible bridge between the protein’s known biochemistry and its observed immunological effect. The significance of DHX15 as a target becomes clear when its normal role is considered. Earlier studies had established that DHX15 cooperates with RIG-I to enhance signaling triggered by RNA viruses, functioning as a co-receptor that strengthens the antiviral response. In other words, DHX15 is not merely an accessory protein; it is part of the amplification system that allows the RIG-I pathway to generate a robust interferon signal. A virus that could disrupt the DHX15-RIG-I partnership would effectively turn down the volume of the alarm before it ever reaches the nucleus. The research team set out to test whether NSP14 does exactly that, and their experiments confirmed the hypothesis. Using co-immunoprecipitation assays, the researchers demonstrated that NSP14 dampens the interaction between DHX15 and RIG-I. By binding to DHX15, the viral protein occupies a partner that would otherwise assist RIG-I in propagating the activation signal downstream to MAVS, the mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein that serves as the platform assembling TBK1 and other signaling components. The consequences of this interference follow a coherent logic: with fewer productive DHX15-RIG-I complexes, reduced activation of TBK1 and IRF3 follows, and the transcription of interferon genes falters. The pathway from viral methyltransferase to blunted cytokine output is thus traced step by step, from protein-protein contact at the level of the sensors to diminished phosphorylation at the level of the kinases to reduced gene expression at the level of the interferon loci. Discover more Biological Sciences CoV-2 Genetics Biotechnology news updates Health Conditions These findings carry several implications for how scientists understand the immune battlefield inside SARS-CoV-2-infected cells. First, they illustrate the economy of viral genomes, in which a single protein performs multiple jobs: the same NSP14 molecule that proofreads and caps the viral RNA also moonlights as an immune antagonist, using its methyltransferase domain for a second, noncanonical purpose. Second, they highlight DHX15 as a newly appreciated node of viral attack, expanding the list of host factors that coronaviruses manipulate and suggesting that the partnership between helicase co-receptors and RIG-I-like receptors is a vulnerability that pathogens have evolved to exploit. Third, they reinforce the picture of SARS-CoV-2 as a virus with a formidable arsenal of evasion strategies, in which early innate immune suppression buys time for viral replication before adaptive immunity can mount an effective response. The study also opens avenues for therapeutic thinking. If NSP14’s N7-methyltransferase activity is required for suppressing interferon production, then inhibitors of that enzymatic function might do double duty, impairing viral RNA capping while simultaneously relieving the brake on innate immunity. Small molecules targeting the methyltransferase domain are already of interest in antiviral drug development, and this work adds an immunological rationale to the enzymatic one. Similarly, approaches that stabilize or mimic the DHX15-RIG-I interaction could, in principle, restore signaling amplitude in infected tissues, although such strategies remain far from clinical application. As with all mechanistic cell culture studies, important caveats apply: the experiments relied on overexpression systems, and confirming that the same interference operates during authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection at physiological protein levels will be an important next step. What the research ultimately delivers is a clearer molecular narrative of how SARS-CoV-2 mutes the body’s first response to infection. The virus does not merely hide its RNA; it actively dismantles the cooperative architecture of the sensing machinery, using NSP14 to pry apart DHX15 and RIG-I and thereby weakening the signal before it can cascade into interferon production. Every element of that cascade, from the helicase partnership at the membrane-associated sensor level to the phosphorylation of TBK1 and IRF3 to the expression of interferon-stimulated genes, is diminished as a result. In mapping this route with biochemical precision, the team at Guizhou Medical University has not only illuminated a specific evasion tactic of a globally significant pathogen but has also underscored a broader lesson of the COVID-19 era: the proteins viruses bring with them are often multitaskers, and understanding their secondary functions may reveal the most consequential battlegrounds of all. supplementary_news.content: As the new school year begins, Tallahassee students face a looming surge of the flu, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The combination, known as "triple-demic," typically peaks during the cooler winter months. According to the Pandemic Mitigation Collaborative's Sept. 25 update, Leon County's COVID-19 prevalence is high . Cases began climbing after Aug. 15, aligning with the start of the new academic semester at Florida State University, Florida A&M University, and Tallahassee State College. "There is a misconception that COVID 'ended,'" FSU College of Medicine Professor Dr. George Rust said to the FSView. "We've had COVID cases and even deaths continuously since the start of the pandemic. It tends to come in waves, and because of immunizations and some people developing immunity from prior infection, the baseline rates and the seasonal surges are lower than they were in 2021 to 2024, but they persist." Flu cases in Tallahassee currently fall in the low-to-medium range. Historically, Florida's flu season runs from October through May. Rust said the cooler months pose a great risk for "triple-demic" illnesses, including the flu, for several reasons. "Cold, dry air or even indoor heated air (also dry) can help the virus to hang in the air longer and to remain alive on surfaces longer," Rust said. "In addition, drying out the lining of the nose can decrease mucous production that traps germs, and can also diminish the response of immune cells in the nose and respiratory tract." More: What students need to know about the 2026 flu season Rust also noted that colder weather keeps people indoors, increasing face-to-face contact. Holiday travel and gatherings bring people together from different areas, allowing viruses to spread easily in crowded, indoor environments. To curb viral transmissions, local healthcare professionals encourage students to establish simple daily routines. "Washing your hands, covering your cough, and using hand sanitizer after touching the gas pump are some simple and easy habits that work to prevent illness not only during flu season but year-round," Megan Waltman, an infection preventionist and nurse at Tallahassee Memorial HealthCare, said to the FSView. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, washing hands with soap for 20 to 30 seconds effectively stops the spread of germs. The habit can reduce respiratory illnesses, such as colds, in the general population by 16% to 21%. Students can take simple steps to stay safe. FSU Assistant Director of Public Relations & Appointment Scheduling at University Health Services (UHS) Mari Kay Avant told the FSView that several daily habits can prevent the spread of respiratory illness. "Students should wash their hands regularly, get enough sleep, eat balanced meals, stay hydrated, and remain physically active," Avant said to the FSView. "It's also important to avoid sharing drinks, utensils, and other personal items. If you do get sick, stay home and limit close contact with others to help prevent spreading illness to friends, roommates, and others on campus." Flu vaccines are currently offered at UHS at no cost to FSU students. To maximize convenience, UHS will host vaccination clinics across campus this semester. Upcoming outreach includes mobile "Flu-ber" stations and the Be Well, Do Well Health Fair on Landis Green on Oct. 1. More: Florida moves to drop four school vaccine requirements Avant said that students who experience symptoms or have health concerns can visit UHS for treatment. Established, returning patients with Patient Portal access can schedule appointments online . First-time patients must call UHS at 850-644-4567 or visit the clinic in person to book a time. All students must bring their FSUCard and health insurance card to check in. Avant added that students seeking same-day appointments should call early in the morning when opening slots are most available. McKinsey Lamm is a Staff Writer for the FSView & Florida Flambeau, the student-run, independent online news service for the FSU and Tallahassee communities. Email our staff at contact@fsview.com . Symptoms Alone Can't Tell: Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD Author(s)Sabrina McCrear, Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD Fact checked by: Rose McNulty Overlapping COVID-19 and flu symptoms make diagnosis hard, says Trinity Health's Tammy Lundstrom, who outlines prevention and vaccine guidance. Advertisement Captions are auto-generated. COVID-19 infections are growing or likely growing in 27 states as of September 16, 2026, according to estimates from the CDC.1 As flu season begins, Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD, senior vice president and chief medical officer at Trinity Health, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® that COVID-19 and flu symptoms overlap enough to make the 2 illnesses difficult to tell apart. Fatigue, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, cough, and shortness of breath are all symptoms associated with both COVID-19 and the flu, Lundstrom said. Children in particular may also experience gastrointestinal upset, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, with COVID-19, she added. "Really, it's hard to distinguish just by symptoms what you're dealing with. It really requires a visit," Lundstrom said. To limit spread, she recommended staying home when sick, washing hands frequently, using antimicrobial hand gels, avoiding touching the nose, mouth, and eyes, and covering the mouth and nose when sneezing or coughing. Lundstrom also emphasized vaccination. She recommended the flu vaccine for anyone aged 6 months and older, with a high-dose or recombinant flu vaccine for adults older than 65 years. For COVID-19, she pointed to recommendations from the Infectious Diseases Society of America, the American Medical Association, and the American Academy of Pediatrics. "Anybody over the age of 19 should get vaccinated. Those 6 months of age to 23 months should be vaccinated for COVID," she explained. "And then older children are really based on their risk profile. And definitely, supporting ACOG's [American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists'] recommendation for vaccination of pregnant women to prevent more severe consequences from COVID." For RSV, Lundstrom recommended vaccination for adults aged 75 years and older, adults aged 50 to 74 years at high risk, and pregnant women. For newborns whose mothers were not vaccinated, monoclonal antibodies can provide protection against RSV, she said. Reference 1. Current Epidemic Trends (Based on Rt). CDC. September 18, 2026. What Parents Should Know Author(s)Sabrina McCrear, Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD Fact checked by: Laura Joszt, MA Listen 0:00 / 0:00 Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD, discusses the new childhood vaccine order, single-dose MMR access concerns, and the measles resurgence. Advertisement As the US records its highest number of measles cases in more than 3 decades, parents heading into fall are also navigating a federal overhaul of childhood vaccine guidance.1 An August executive order narrowed the list of diseases that all children should be vaccinated against from 18 to 11, moving influenza, COVID-19, hepatitis A and B, rotavirus, and meningococcal disease to shared clinical decision-making or risk-based recommendations. At the same time, measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination coverage among kindergartners slipped to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, while exemptions reached a record 4.2%.2 In an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® (AJMC®), Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD, senior vice president and chief medical officer at Trinity Health, discussed what these changes mean for families, why she sees single-dose MMR shots as an access problem, and how clinicians can build trust with hesitant parents. This interview has been lightly edited for clarity. AJMC: The August executive order narrows the list of diseases that all children are recommended to be vaccinated against to 11. It moves flu, COVID-19, hepatitis A and B, rotavirus, and meningococcal disease to shared clinical decision-making or risk-based recommendations. What does that mean for a parent trying to decide what their child needs this fall? Lundstrom: We're still following the previous recommendations and following the science. I think we've always, at least in my estimation, had shared decision-making for vaccines as providers, discussing with our patients the risks and benefits and the risks of not getting vaccinated, which are consequential, especially now with the measles outbreaks that we're seeing. Really, it's talking to parents about that. With hepatitis B for infants, I am old enough to have practiced in the era when we didn't have these vaccines, and I saw a lot of chronic liver disease in babies whose moms were hepatitis B carriers. Really, it's about having that conversation so that people truly understand from a scientific perspective what the risks and benefits are. AJMC: The order also calls for childhood vaccines to be given as single-disease shots rather than combination products when feasible, starting with splitting the MMR vaccine into 3 separate shots. From a clinical and access standpoint, what's your take on that? Lundstrom: I think from an access standpoint, it's problematic. We already know there's difficulty with getting access, and if you're talking about 3 visits instead of 1, that's taking parents away from work, trying to get 3 different appointments versus 1. I think the IDSA [Infectious Diseases Society of America] and American Academy of Pediatrics would agree that there's no benefit, from a scientific perspective, of getting 3 different injections versus 1. I think most pediatricians and most infectious disease doctors are still recommending getting the combined dose. The separate doses aren't even available in the US right now, so that complicates access and the recommendations. AJMC: The US is seeing its highest number of measles cases in more than 30 years, and nonmedical exemptions among kindergartners rose to 4.0% in the 2025-2026 school year. How worried are you about pockets of undervaccinated children, and what should a parent do if their child may have been exposed to measles? Lundstrom: I'm very worried about that, because I just saw data today from KFF showing that 92.4% of kindergartners are now vaccinated for MMR. And measles is one of the most contagious diseases that we have. We need at least 95% vaccination rates to provide herd immunity.2 That is very scary and problematic, especially in light of what I just heard today: Pennsylvania is nearing 800 cases, which is very, very concerning.4 I think if children are behind in vaccinations, now is a good time to get caught up. And if they've been exposed to measles, communicating with either public health or your primary care provider about the best options to try to prevent disease is the way to go. AJMC: You've led Trinity Health's pandemic response and spoken at town halls to counter misinformation. What approach works best when a hesitant parent comes to you with questions, and how do you keep trust when federal guidance and groups like the American Academy of Pediatrics are giving different advice? Lundstrom: It's really about the conversation, trying to understand people's fears. What are they afraid of? Do they understand the consequences if their child or somebody in their family gets one of these vaccine-preventable diseases? Many people are young enough that they haven't experienced the terrible consequences that can happen with some of these vaccine-preventable illnesses. Having factual conversations and trying to lay out the facts and the science is the best way to go forward. And then, like I said, try to understand the individual fear and address that. And myth-bust, too. We've done town halls, and we have myth-busting. A lot of what’s on social media isn’t scientifically accurate, so we’re trying to make sure people have the right information to make their decision. References Measles cases and outbreaks. CDC. Milbank Q.2026;104(4):0912. https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-0009.70130 Related Content: Reforming Physician Licensure in the United States to Improve Access to Telehealth: State, Regional, and Federal Initiatives Quarterly Article December 2024 Changing US Support for Public Health Data Uses through Pandemic and Political Turmoil Quarterly Article June 2024 Public Health Emergency Preparedness After COVID-19 Quarterly Article The Future of Population Health Back to The Milbank Quarterly Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... Policy Points: Institutional trust appears to constitute an essential component of pandemic preparedness. Czech excess mortality—49% higher than Austria’s and approximately twice the European mean—illustrates that governance failures can undermine functional preparedness assets. The observed 8–10-week lag between trust decline and mortality divergence is consistent with a potential early-warning window. Regular monitoring of public trust may identify governance deterioration before preventable mortality escalates, thereby operationalizing trust as a measurable governance outcome. Competent health leadership continuity is a protective factor, not a guarantee. Five Czech health ministers in 15 months coincided with the deterioration in public cooperation, demonstrating how political instability weakens pandemic-response capacities even where technical preparedness exists. Context: The Czech Republic’s COVID-19 excess mortality represents a preparedness paradox. Despite entering the pandemic with substantial technical capacity—including the highest intensive care unit density in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, an early national mask mandate, and an initially effective contact-tracing system—that country experienced age-standardized excess mortality of 15.24 per 10,000, approximately twice the European mean and 49% higher than neighboring Austria. Methods: This mixed-methods comparative case analysis examined relevant data from March 2020 through December 2023. Austria was chosen as a comparative governance benchmark to the Czech Republic because it closely matched that country’s initial governmental trust level (entering the pandemic within approximately two percentage points), and Slovakia is a historically and geographically proximate comparator. Age-standardized excess mortality was examined alongside government trust measures, mobility indicators, vaccination data, and policy stringency indices. Exploratory lag correlations assessed the temporal relationship between changes in trust and subsequent mortality. Findings: Czech governmental trust declined from approximately 71% to 19% during the pandemic period, among the largest declines in Europe. Austrian trust remained comparatively stable, whereas Slovakia also experienced a substantial decline in trust alongside high excess mortality. Czech mortality divergence from Austria emerged approximately 8–10 weeks after trust deterioration. Four mechanisms are proposed through which trust erosion may have influenced mortality: reduced compliance with public health measures, vaccine hesitancy, collapse of contact tracing, and governance-associated misperceptions of the scientific consensus. Conclusions: This analysis suggests that governance stability and institutional trust appear to function as important public health pandemic preparedness measures. supplementary_news.content: News Sports Autos Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Michigan, much of the U.S. in COVID-19 surge Kristen Jordan Shamus Detroit Free Press Sept. 23, 2026, 5:01 p.m. ET Hear this story The Pandemic Mitigation Collaboration analyzes wastewater data to show where COVID-19 is spreading most. This week, its updated map shows Michigan is now in a surge. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has changed the way it reports data on COVID-19, lowering the thresholds for what is considered low, moderate, high and very high levels. Experts suggest the time is now to get a COVID-19 vaccine, if you haven't already. As Michiganders weigh their seasonal vaccine options, COVID-19 cases are surging close to home and across much of the U.S. The Mitten is among at least 37 states and three territories are experiencing coronavirus outbreaks, according to the Pandemic Mitigation Collaborative's latest map, which was built using county-by-county data from wastewater samples. It notes: There likely are outbreaks in other states, too, where monitoring is poor, such as Maryland, Idaho, Louisiana and Tennessee. Here in Michigan, testing of wastewater samples from six Michigan communities show more people in the state had COVID-19 infections in the last week than at any time since March, according to WastewaterSCAN. Coronavirus activity was considered "high" as of Sept. 16 at collection sites in Ann Arbor, the city of Warren and Mount Pleasant. It was considered "moderate" in Jackson, Jenison and Traverse City, though the data suggests an upward trend. This means now is the time to get a COVID-19 vaccine, if you haven't already been boosted this season, said Michael Hoerger, who leads the collaborative at Tulane University, where he also is an associate professor of psychology, psychiatry and oncology. What type of COVID-19 vaccine should I get? The U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized the following COVID-19 vaccines, which have been updated for the 2026-27 respiratory virus: Nuvaxovid: A protein-based vaccine made by Novavax and Sanofi, which can be used in people ages 65 and older as well as those between the ages of 12 and 64 with an underlying condition, such as asthma, cancer, diabetes or obesity, that puts them at higher risk for severe outcomes from COVID-19. Spikevax, an mRNA vaccine made by Moderna, which can be given to people ages 65 or older and to those who are between 6 months and 64 years old with at least one underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe outcomes from COVID-19. Comirnaty, an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine made by Pfizer and BioNTech. It can be used in people ages 65 and older as well as anyone ranging from 5 years to 64 years old with at least one underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe outcomes from COVID-19. mNexSpike, a lower-dose mRNA COVID-19 vaccine made by Moderna that can be used in people ages 65 and older as well as those between the ages of 12 and 64 who have an underlying condition that puts them at risk for severe disease with COVID-19 infection. CDC shifts how it reports COVID-19 spread Tracking COVID-19 spread six years after the pandemic began isn't as easy as it used to be, as reporting requirements have changed along with the way the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention maps the virus on its website. The federal agency has shifted its analysis of wastewater data in a way that minimizes the risk of infection, said Hoerger. "The CDC is blue washing to make COVID levels look artificially low," Hoerger said in a video posted on the collaborative's website. "They changed their color-coding scheme to make COVID levels look lower across the U.S. and there are further data anomalies that raise red flags. All of this leaves you less prepared. "The CDC monitors COVID transmission through wastewater and they take these numeric values and convert them to a color scheme in categories. About a year ago, they made a major update to the system that mostly pushed higher levels into lower categories. This [August], they did the exact same thing, but to a much greater degree." So, he explained, a level of COVID detection in wastewater that would have been considered very high in the past is now classified as just "high" on the CDC's surveillance map. Similarly, "moderate" spread is now considered "low," which is represented on the CDC's map as the color blue. "The CDC website is just less reliable for the casual user," Hoerger said. "We warned you that if any funny business like this ever happened, we would catch it right away. Here, we did." Hoerger and his team developed a heat map that shows county-by-county COVID-19 transmission using raw data collected from wastewater samples that can reveal a clearer picture of how much of the virus is spreading in communities, he said. It allows people to see the data the way it used to be classified, and to toggle to the system the CDC now is using to compare the differences. Changing federal vaccine recommendations, too It isn't only the data about COVID-19 spread that's changed at a federal level. President Donald Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. secretary of health and human services, have made dramatic changes to how the U.S. government reviews and recommends vaccines and issues guidelines for their use. Those efforts have sparked outrage among many in the scientific community, which led the major medical societies and associations to band together in collaboration with the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota to launch the Vaccine Integrity Project, which provides evidence-based data on the safety and efficacy of vaccines. “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories,'' said Sarah C. Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) during an August news conference. "They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives." Although they differ from the federal government's guidelines on COVID-19 vaccines, the AAFP's recommendations are closely aligned with those set by other medical societies, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the American Medical Association, "to ensure continuity for both patients and physicians," Nosal said. Dr. Ronald Nahass, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, said at the news conference that all of the organizations are "speaking with one voice relative to the vaccinations and all acknowledging the challenges of the lack of trust and the lack of clarity. "The medical community ... is uniform in our effort to bring clarity and to restore that trust." They suggest: All adults 19 years of age and older should get an annual COVID-19 vaccine. It is especially important to get a COVID-19 vaccine if you are: 65 years and older; At an increased risk for severe COVID-19 infection; and Have never received a COVID-19 vaccine. All adults ages 65 years and older should get two doses of the updated COVID-19 vaccine. The first should be administered this fall. The second shot should follow six months later to maintain protection against the virus because immunity wanes over time. Infants and toddlers between the ages 6 months and 23 months should be vaccinated against COVID-19. Kids ages 2 years to 18 years old who are at risk for severe illness from COVID-19 infection should be vaccinated. The same is true for any children whose families choose to vaccinate against COVID-19. Anyone who is pregnant should get a COVID-19 vaccine during any trimester. Vaccination also is safe for women who are breast-feeding. Contact Kristen Shamus: kshamus@freepress.com. Subscribe to the Detroit Free Press.
